strengths: Clever factorization approach that exploits hierarchical structure of CSLs to enable efficient exhaustive search, reducing O(|XD|) neural network evaluations to manageable computation
Impressive engineering achieving 30-second queries on 10B compounds with single T4 GPU, making interactive exploration feasible
Proper experimental methodology with ground-truth evaluation on 12M fully-enumerated library and careful handling of data leakage (trained on 1M, tested on 12M/10B)
Comprehensive evaluation across 5 protein targets and 5 constraint sets, with consistent high recall performance (0.7-0.8 for top-100 with k=100k budget)
Valuable contribution of open-source benchmark CSL for reproducibility in drug discovery screening research
Clear mathematical formulation with concrete computational complexity analysis (1 trillion operation example)
weaknesses: Missing critical baseline comparisons: V-SYNTHES and NGT mentioned but never compared; Thompson sampling evaluation restricted to only 5 reactions (~4M compounds) and unconstrained case only, limiting assessment

Surrogate error propagation not rigorously analyzed: No sensitivity study showing how prediction errors translate to retrieval quality; assumes minimizing surrogate MSE ensures good top-k recovery without validation
Factorizer approximation quality not quantified: Reconstruction error for Eq. 12 never reported; unclear how factorization error compounds surrogate error and affects final retrieval quality
All evaluation restricted to synthetic BRICS-based CSL: No validation on actual make-on-demand libraries (Enamine REAL, ChemSpace); generalization to real-world settings undemonstrated
Insufficient ablation studies: No justification for specific architectural choices (e.g., bilinear form in Eq. 10); no comparison of surrogate architectures or factorizer depth sensitivity
Weak errors-in-variables robustness justification: Noise added during training but absent at test time; connection to robustness needs rigorous theoretical justification
Limited scope: Single scoring function (AutoDock Vina) and property predictions only; no multi-objective optimization, Pareto frontier exploration, or computationally expensive scoring functions
Practical significance of recall metrics unclear: 0.7-0.8 recall for top-100 shown, but missing analysis of how close misses are in score space and impact on drug discovery workflows
Constraint handling analysis incomplete: No quantification of false positive/negative rates for APEX predictions vs ground truth constraints
Implementation details sparse: Factorizer training curves, convergence behavior, and computational cost of surrogate/factorizer training not reported; code not yet available

strengths: Addresses a compelling practical problem: enabling exhaustive evaluation of ultra-large CSLs (billions of compounds) is a genuine bottleneck in drug discovery, and the achieved speedup (full library in ~30 seconds on single T4 GPU) is practically significant

Novel and clever technical approach: The hierarchical factorization strategy that exploits combinatorial structure through synthon contributions is creative and well-motivated, achieving remarkable computational efficiency (3 TFLOP vs. 3 trillion for naive approach)

Sound mathematical framework: Clear problem formulation (Eq. 1-2), well-motivated surrogate parameterization with noise-augmented training for robustness to errors-in-variables (Eq. 4), and correct factorization derivation (Eq. 13-17)

Valuable benchmark contribution: Open, fully-enumerated 10B+ compound CSL with exhaustive docking scores for 5 diverse protein targets and physicochemical properties; proper train/test split (1M/12M/10B) prevents data leakage

Strong empirical results on tested comparisons: Achieves 70%+ recall for top-100 compounds with k=100,000 budget (0.8% of library); consistently outperforms Thompson sampling with matched budgets; effective constraint satisfaction across multiple drug-likeness rules

High-quality implementation: Custom GPU implementation using CCCL with chain-of-batches strategy and efficient top-k retrieval demonstrates engineering rigor; clear algorithmic description in Appendix A.3
Clear presentation: Well-motivated introduction, logical flow from problem through methodology to experiments; helpful visualizations (Figure 2 overview, Figure 4 enrichment analysis)
weaknesses: Limited baseline comparisons: Only compares against Thompson sampling and random baseline; missing comparisons with V-SYNTHES (hierarchical method) and NGT (generative approach) mentioned in introduction; TS comparison restricted to top 5 reactions (~4M compounds) not full library; claims of 'consistently strong performance' somewhat overstated

Surrogate model accuracy underexplored: Figure 7 shows R² for docking scores ranges 0.4-0.7, indicating substantial prediction error (60% variance unexplained for some targets); missing sensitivity analysis on how retrieval quality degrades with lower surrogate accuracy; no analysis of which targets/objectives perform poorly

Generalization to new libraries unclear: Surrogate trained only on 1M compounds from single CSL design (ZINC22-based BRICS); evaluated only on downsamples of same design; would approach work for Enamine REAL or different fragment libraries? Retraining needs for new objectives unknown; severely limits practical applicability

Factorization approximation error not thoroughly analyzed: Figure 7 shows factorized surrogate R² drops relative to original; this compounds with surrogate error but impact on retrieval quality not quantified; reconstruction error (Eq. 12) and its practical implications not explored

Lack of experimental validation: CSL is synthetically constructed and not validated on commercial libraries; no synthesis/testing of predicted compounds; docking scores from AutoDock Vina correlation with actual binding unknown; cannot claim real drug discovery utility

Missing ablation studies: No ablation on noise in surrogate training (Eq. 4); no ablation on factorizer architecture; embedding dimension d=64 stated as 'not extensively tuned'—what's the sensitivity? Cannot identify critical components

Computational cost breakdown incomplete: Runtime reported only for search phase (Table 1); missing surrogate training time, factorizer training time, and full pipeline cost; for practitioners considering adoption, total cost including initial setup is critical

Evaluation metrics limited: Primary metric is Recall-j-at-k; missing ranking quality metrics (NDCG); no analysis of retrieved set diversity (clustering of solutions); no enrichment factor analysis beyond CDF visualization

Reproducibility concerns: Code and data promised but not provided for review; neural network architecture details sparse (layer counts, activations, initialization); training procedures incomplete (optimizer details, hyperparameters, convergence criteria); difficult for independent reproduction

Theoretical analysis informal: Error-in-variables robustness explained intuitively but lacks formal bounds; no characterization of when factorization approximation is valid; linearity assumption in embedding space not formally justified; error propagation through pipeline not rigorously analyzed

strengths: Sound technical approach: Factorization strategy is mathematically elegant and well-motivated for CSL structure; noise-based training addresses errors-in-variables robustness
Comprehensive evaluation with ground truth: Benchmark CSL with 10M+ exhaustively docked compounds across 5 targets enables quantitative retrieval accuracy metrics beyond surrogate proxies
Impressive practical performance: 10B compound library screened in <30 seconds on single GPU enables new screening workflows unavailable to prior methods
Principled amortization: One-time training enables arbitrary objective/constraint modifications without retraining, unlike generative approaches requiring policy reoptimization per query
Error decomposition validates design: Appendix A.6 demonstrates surrogate and factorizer errors are largely independent, justifying two-stage approach
Zero-shot generalization: Application to Enamine REAL (70B compounds) despite training only on BRICS shows non-trivial transfer capability
Reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, architecture specifications, and commitment to code/data release
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Combines existing techniques (neural surrogates, factorization machines from Rendle 2010, hierarchical encoders from Pedawi et al. 2022) without fundamental algorithmic innovation

Incomplete experimental comparisons: Only Thompson Sampling comparison on 5 reactions (~4M compounds, not 10B); no comparison with Deep Docking, MolPal, MEMES mentioned in related work; no comparison with embedding methods (DrugCLIP/ConPLex claiming million-fold speedups); TS comparison restricted to unconstrained case

Moderate surrogate quality: R²~0.6-0.7 for docking scores indicates substantial prediction error; linear probes on frozen embeddings is restrictive without justification; zero-shot Enamine performance degrades significantly (MET: 0.6→0.4 R²); total NMSE can be substantial (Figure 8)

Synthetic benchmark lacks validation: CSL constructed from ZINC22 with BRICS, acknowledges no synthetic feasibility verification; no experimental/wet-lab validation that APEX-retrieved compounds outperform alternatives; ground truth is computational docking (unreliable proxy)

Missing critical ablations: No ablation of factorizer hierarchy components; no comparison of linear vs. nonlinear probes subject to factorization constraints; no sensitivity to noise level; no analysis of when/why factorization assumption holds

Moderate absolute performance: Figure 2A shows recall of top-100 is ~40-60% even with k=100,000 (0.8% budget); counter-screening constraints substantially degrade absolute objective performance (Figure 11)
Unjustified design choices: Why linear probes vs. constrained nonlinear? Why isotropic normal noise? Why RgroupKeyEncoder takes both R-group and reaction embeddings? No sensitivity analyses
Scope limitations: Method requires explicit CSL structure (synthons/R-groups/reactions); still requires 1M labeled compounds for surrogate training; not compared against most recent embedding methods
